title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles

epigraph.quote: Our company has survived by solving problems that almost put us out of business every five years. The secret of NVIDIA is that we were willing to suffer through thirty years of skepticism to build a computing platform that the world would eventually find indispensable.
epigraph.author: Jensen Huang, Co-Founder and CEO, Stanford Graduate School of Business Address (2024)

web_blocks.html: NVIDIA was founded in April 1993 at a Denny's diner in San Jose. California, by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem. The three computer scientists recognized that the central processing unit CPU. Designed for general-purpose sequential computing. Was fundamentally ill-suited for the complex. Parallel mathematical calculations required by real-time 3D computer graphics. While Intel and the broader semiconductor industry focused on increasing CPU clock frequencies. NVIDIA wagered that specialized parallel processing would enable photorealistic visual computing. That foundational insight launched a thirty-year corporate trajectory characterized by near-death existential crises. Radical platform pivots. The company also capital allocation gambles that fundamentally transformed computing architecture.

The company's initial commercial product. The NV1 chip launched in 1995, integrated 2D video, 3D graphics, audio. The company also gaming console controllers onto a single silicon die using quadratic texture mapping. It was an ambitious technical marvel but an absolute commercial disaster. When Microsoft released Direct3D in 1996 based on polygonal rendering rather than quadratic surfaces. The NV1 was instantly obsolete. NVIDIA burned through its venture capital, laid off half its workforce. It also survived on a critical $5 million development contract from Sega to build the graphics processor for the Dreamcast console. Facing imminent bankruptcy. Jensen Huang abandoned quadratic surfaces, pivoted the remaining engineering team to standard polygonal geometry. At the same time, released the RIVA 128 graphics accelerator in 1997. The RIVA 128 was an immediate commercial triumph. Selling one million units in its first four months and funding the company's January 1999 initial public offering on the NASDAQ.

web_blocks.title: The CUDA Capital Allocation Bet: Sunk Cost or Asymmetric Option?
paragraphs: In 2006, NVIDIA made what Wall Street universally condemned as a value-destroying capital allocation blunder: the development and universal integration of CUDA Compute Unified Device Architecture. CUDA exposed the parallel computing cores of graphics chips to general software developers using standard C and C++ extensions.

For six consecutive years from 2006 through 2012. NVIDIA added CUDA silicon logic and software overhead to every consumer GPU shipped. Spending billions in cumulative gross margin penalties and specialized developer tooling. Wall Street questioned why a consumer PC gaming component maker was subsidizing academic researchers and oil-and-gas seismic modelers. That patient six-year capital sink created the global software moat that later powered modern deep learning when AlexNet ran convolutional neural networks on two consumer GeForce GTX 580 GPUs in 2012.

web_blocks.html: NVIDIA's financial history reveals distinct boom-and-bust operating cycles. Driven through underlying technology transitions and inventory bullwhips. Between 2017 and 2019, the surge in cryptocurrency mining created insatiable demand for GeForce gaming GPUs. This pushed annual revenue from $6.91 billion in fiscal 2017 to $11.72 billion in fiscal 2019. When crypto prices collapsed in late 2018, secondary markets were flooded with discounted GPUs. This caused channel inventory to back up across global distributors. NVIDIA was forced to take a massive $1.2 billion inventory write-down. Quarterly gaming revenue plummeted by more than 45%. The company also the company took four full quarters to digest excess channel inventory. That crisis taught management an invaluable lesson about channel visibility, inventory commitments. It also the risk of uncommitted end-demand.

Rather than retrenching, management capitalized on the crypto trough to execute the most strategically important acquisition in enterprise technology history: the April 2020 acquisition of Mellanox Technologies for $6.9 billion in cash. Competitors viewed Mellanox as a niche provider of high-speed InfiniBand switches and network adapters for national supercomputers. Jensen Huang recognized that individual silicon chips had reached physical limits, and that the future unit of computing would be an entire data center. By marrying graphics processors with Mellanox's ultra-low-latency InfiniBand and RoCE networking fabric. NVIDIA built the end-to-end full-stack computing engine required to train trillion-parameter artificial intelligence models.

The launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT in November 2022 marked the watershed moment when thirty years of full-stack investment intersected with a generational platform shift. As hyperscalers, national governments. The company also frontier research labs rushed to build accelerated computing clusters. NVIDIA's Data Center revenue exploded from $15.0 billion in fiscal 2023 to $47.5 billion in fiscal 2024. $115.2 billion in fiscal 2025. It also reached $193.7 billion in fiscal 2026. Total company revenue expanded thirty-fold over the decade from $5.01 billion in fiscal 2016 to $215.94 billion in fiscal 2026. Establishing NVIDIA as the primary infrastructure foundation of modern accelerated enterprise computing.

web_blocks.html: A pivotal yet frequently overlooked chapter in NVIDIA's corporate evolution was its strategic failure in mobile smartphones between 2011 and 2015. Following the initial success of the Tegra mobile processor in early Android tablets. NVIDIA attempted to compete head-to-head with Qualcomm through integrating cellular baseband modems into mobile system-on-chips SoCs. After acquiring Icera for $367 million in 2011 to secure modem IP. NVIDIA struggled against Qualcomm's integrated Snapdragon platform and Apple's in-house silicon. Recognizing that consumer smartphone silicon was rapidly commoditizing into a low-margin merchant business with extreme carrier certification barriers. Jensen Huang made the painful decision to write down the modem investment. Exit the mobile smartphone market entirely. The company also pivot the Tegra architecture into automotive infotainment, autonomous robotics. In addition, Nintendo Switch gaming consoles.

That forced exit from smartphones proved to be a blessing in disguise. Had NVIDIA succeeded in becoming a high-volume mobile chip supplier. Its engineering talent and research capital would have been consumed by annual smartphone iteration cycles and carrier price negotiations. By abandoning mobile, management freed up hundreds of senior software engineers and millions of dollars in silicon research budgets to focus exclusively on high-performance computing, deep neural network training. The company also datacenter interconnect fabrics. The corporate resilience forged through abandoning mobile commoditization directly enabled the accelerated computing breakthroughs that followed.

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand NVIDIA. You and I have to begin not in the server racks of Ashburn or Santa Clara, but in the booth of a twenty-four-hour roadside diner in San Jose in the spring of 1993. Three engineers sat over lukewarm coffee. Sketching out an architecture for three-dimensional graphics that almost everyone in Silicon Valley believed was commercially unviable. The prevailing orthodoxy of the semiconductor world was governed by Moore's Law as interpreted by Andy Grove and Intel: sequential central processing units would double their clock speeds every eighteen months. The company also software compilers would simply ride that wave. The notion that computer users needed an entirely separate coprocessor dedicated to parallel floating-point arithmetic was dismissed as an expensive toy for niche video game enthusiasts.

What Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem grasped was a fundamental law of physics that sequential processors could not escape. Rendering three dimensions on a two-dimensional screen requires computing millions of polygons simultaneously for every single frame. Thirty to sixty times per second. Increasing CPU clock frequencies generated exponential heat dissipation without solving the intrinsic serial bottleneck. Specialized parallel hardware, operating hundreds of simpler arithmetic cores in lockstep, was the only mathematical answer. That conviction led to the founding of NVIDIA, but conviction without execution in hardware engineering is a swift path to liquidation.

The company's first chip, the NV1, was an unmitigated disaster that nearly extinguished the enterprise before it took breath. Huang had wagered on quadratic texture mapping at the exact moment Microsoft established polygonal geometry as the industry standard with Direct3D. When you build the wrong chip in hardware, you cannot issue an over-the-air patch. You have committed millions of dollars in photomasks and silicon foundry wafers that cannot be sold. With thirty days of payroll remaining in the bank. Huang laid off half his staff and staked the company's survival on the RIVA 128. A polygonal processor engineered on a shoestring budget. When that chip launched in 1997, it became a runaway hit. Survival, for NVIDIA, was forged in the fire of immediate commercial failure.

Nine years later. This comes with the company solidly profitable as the premier graphics card supplier for PC gamers. Huang made the single most scrutinized capital allocation decision of his career. In 2006, he mandated that Compute Unified Device Architecture—CUDA—must be built into every single GPU shipped by the company, free of charge to software developers. For six straight years, Wall Street analysts questioned why NVIDIA was penalizing its gross margins through dedicating precious silicon real estate and hundreds of software engineers to an enterprise that generated zero direct revenue. Huang endured that skepticism because he saw that hardware without an embedded software compiler is a commodity. Whereas hardware coupled to a proprietary software ecosystem becomes an unbreakable standard.

When artificial intelligence researchers discovered in 2012 that convolutional neural networks could be trained on NVIDIA's CUDA cores in days rather than months. Thirty years of patient, unglamorous platform development suddenly ignited into a generational monopoly. As you examine the company today. Remember that this massive infrastructure enterprise was built not through serendipity, but through repeated existential survival and an unmatched willingness to absorb capital penalties to control the software interface of computing.

When you study the history of great technology corporations. You often discover that their most valuable strategic victories were born from their most painful public defeats. In the early 2010s, every semiconductor executive in Silicon Valley believed that the consumer smartphone was the only market that mattered. If you were not shipping hundreds of millions of chips into Apple iPhones or Samsung Galaxy handsets. Wall Street viewed you as an evolutionary dead end. Jensen Huang attempted to play that game with the Tegra processor and the acquisition of Icera modems. The company also he was decisively beaten by Qualcomm's patent portfolio and ruthless carrier integration.

Imagine the psychological fortitude required to stand before your board of directors and institutional shareholders in 2014 and announce that you are writing off hundreds of millions of dollars of modem investments and walking away from the largest consumer electronics market in human history. Weaker corporate leaders would have doubled down. Chasing low-margin socket wins at five percent gross margins simply to show headline revenue growth. Huang walked away because he realized that commodity consumer sockets destroy economic value.

Instead, he redeployed those engineering teams into high-performance parallel computing. While competitors were grinding away designing slightly thinner smartphone application processors. NVIDIA was building the mathematical libraries that would eventually train transformer models. In business. As a result, in portfolio management, the decision of what not to do is often ten times more important than the decision of what to pursue.

That episode teaches you and me an invaluable lesson about management temperament. A great chief executive does not avoid mistakes. They recognize strategic dead ends quickly, liquidate them without ego. The company also pivot remaining resources toward uncrowded, asymmetric technological frontiers.

Reflect on how different computing history might look today if Jensen Huang had chosen the path of least resistance during the mid-2000s. If management had prioritized short-term operating profit and deferred the development of CUDA. Graphics processors would have remained specialized gaming peripherals. The company also the artificial intelligence revolution would have been delayed by a decade.

This long-term orientation is what venture capitalists call patient capital, but inside a publicly traded corporation, it requires executive courage. Huang withstood years of critical research reports from Wall Street analysts who argued that CUDA was a distraction from core gaming markets. That willingness to endure public skepticism to build a long-term architectural platform is the hallmark of founder-led excellence.

When you look back across three decades of semiconductor innovation. Notice that NVIDIA is one of the very few Silicon Valley enterprises still led by its founding chief executive. That unbroken continuity of vision and operational paranoia is a rare asset that cannot be quantified in quarterly financial filings.

Notice how the early partnership with video game developers like Epic Games and id Software established NVIDIA's developer-first DNA. By providing graphics programmers with direct access to hardware engineers and writing custom software drivers to eliminate performance bugs in major gaming titles. NVIDIA built an enduring reservoir of goodwill across the software engineering community. That cultural tradition of subordinating hardware to software developer productivity continues to govern enterprise customer relationships today.

book_callouts.title: The Strategic Discipline of Full-Stack Architecture
book_callouts.text: Notice how NVIDIA never viewed itself merely as a semiconductor design house. While rivals sold standalone silicon dies to board manufacturers, NVIDIA consistently built the compilers, the mathematical libraries, the networking fabrics, and the system reference designs. By controlling the entire stack from transistor to algorithmic runtime, the company eliminated the risk of becoming a commoditized component supplier.
